content.thinking:
I'm planning the proportions and pose for the red panda model, standing on a mossy stone with its head raised and tail curved upward, and starting to work out the coordinate layout.

Now I'm shaping the stone itself, trying a lathe profile to get a flatter, more natural rock-like top instead of a plain sphere, adjusting the radius and height points so the panda's feet sit properly on the surface.

one stone cel-shaded with moss accumulation based on normal direction and noise, with shadowing derived from the lighting setup. I'll scatter moss tufts and small clumps on top for texture, then move to the panda skeleton: hips around 0.47-0.48m up with short legs, and a back line running from hips to shoulders.

I'm now working out proportions -- body length, chest and rump positions, leg lengths relative to the stone height, and belly clearance above the feet, adjusting until the legs read as appropriately short but not awkward. Then I'm laying out the spine as a chain of joints from hips to neck base, figuring out how many named segments the catmull path needs and how the root hip joint should connect to the first spine joint.

Setting up a radius array for smooth body tapering, then defining a neck chain running from the spine's end up toward the head, with two spans named neck1/neck2 parented to spine3, and placing the head joint angled upward.

Now I'm picking the fur palette—burnt orange, deep rust, dark brown underside, and cream—then applying countershading so the belly reads darker than the back, with a furred edge texture layered on top for the coat.

For the legs, I'm setting up IK chains: front legs bend backward at the elbow, hind legs have a three-segment chain bending forward at the knee and back at the hock, with shoulder/hip anchor points and foot targets positioned to get natural standing proportions.

Checking the foot placement against the stone's surface profile to make sure the paws sink slightly into it rather than floating, adjusting the foot center height to about 0.328 for a believable contact point.

Writing sweep code for leg tubes...

For the paws, I'm sizing a flattened sphere positioned at the foot joint with a slight forward offset, colored dark brown, then adding small cream claw spikes angled forward-down from the paw front, skipping individual toe beans for simplicity, and mirroring everything across the x-axis using the side sign for left/right limbs. For the tail, I'm sketching a path that roots at the hips and arcs upward and back in a curl reminiscent of the reference image, rising to about 0.98 in height with a forward-curving tip, giving it roughly 0.6 units of total length.

I'm defining the tail's five joints with tapering radii, then painting alternating rust and tan stripe rings along its length using a sweep function keyed to position, adding a zigzag wobble to the ring boundaries for a furry edge look, and darkening the very tip. I'm also considering scattering a few pointy tuft cards along the tail to break up its silhouette, though I need to work out how their coloring should sample from the tail's paint function.

Since cards sample position at the origin by default, I'm switching to simple solid-tinted tuft shapes instead—rust-colored tufts scattered on the body and tan ones elsewhere, keeping the count moderate around 70 cards, tinted via a color string that blends with the cel-shaded lighting. Now I'm moving on to the head, placing a scaled skull sphere at the head joint using world-space coordinates and offset arrays to position the head center slightly above and forward of the neck, keeping the geometry axis-aligned with just a slight upward tilt.

Next I'm adding the snout as a cream-colored sphere, a small dark nose sphere, and a separate jaw joint with its own lower jaw sphere since I want a distinct mouth. Then I'm working out the face paint logic directly on the skull sphere in world coordinates—defining cream cheek and muzzle regions, a small cream brow patch above the eye, and dark tear-line markings running from the eyes down toward the mouth using conditional checks on the local x and y offsets.

Figuring out eye placement using spherical coordinates on the skull surface with amber iris decals, then moving on to designing the ears as big triangular shapes, cream inside and rust outside, with white fur tufts matching the reference.

Adding dark-rust outer ears with cream inner detail, then placing a few cream fur spikes at the cheeks and a rust ruff on the head top, plus thin cream-white whisker rods extending from the muzzle.

Now I'm working out the chest bib, positioning a small cream sphere scaled flat near the neck/chest to suggest a collar marking, while planning the rust-and-tan neck ruff and other body markings.

For texture, I'm scattering roughly 140 orange tufts across the body surface, filtering by height so they only appear on the upper body, using a simple leaf-shaped SVG tuft tinted to a rust-orange with randomized lean and bend for a natural fluffy look.

For the tail ring coloring, I realize I can't easily tie paint to the position along the tail path since I don't have direct access to the parametric t value from hit position, so I'm considering projecting the hit point onto the tail path to recover that t value instead.

Since computing closestT per texel during baking would be too expensive, I decide to compute it only once per scattered card instance, grouping cards by ring parity to alternate tan and rust tints, with a darker tip and rust base at the ends. I'm working out the banding formula so rings alternate roughly every 0.1 unit of t with a zigzag perturbation for a natural edge, then wrapping the cel-shaded paint result through the lighting resolver.

For the moss on the stone, I'm scattering cross-card clumps on upward-facing surfaces using a bumpy circle-cluster SVG tinted in two greens, standing them upright along the surface normal with random lean. I'm also planning small mushroom decorations built from a cylindrical stem and conical cap.

I'm placing a couple mushrooms near the stone's front-left edge, computing their position on the stone's curved top surface, with a red cap and white dots sitting above a thin stem. For the stone itself, I'm deciding whether to attach it directly to the hips joint since it's static, or create a separate "base" joint—leaning toward reusing hips since the pose is static anyway. I'm also working out how to get an elliptical lathe shape for the stone since the built-in lathe helper doesn't support non-uniform scaling, so I may need to build the geometry manually with a scale vector.

Writing stone paint function...

I'm also planning to scatter a few extra grey rock lumps as flat-shaded spheres around the base for a rougher look, add a smaller secondary stone nearby, and sprinkle moss on top, then move on to detailing the eye decal next.

For some Genshin-style flair, I'm thinking of adding a teal ribbon collar swept around the neck with a small golden charm disc and tassel hanging from the front, positioning it using the neck sweep's loop and surface placement.

I'm also considering a thin gold band wrapped around the base of the tail for a matching accessory.

I'll scatter a few tiny glowing green octahedron motes near the head, around heights 0.7-0.85, to echo an elemental motif without overcrowding the silhouette. Then I'm mapping out the tail's curved path as a sequence of points rising and curling forward over the back, peaking around y 1.04, matching the reference pose where the tail arcs up and over.

That total height with the raised tail feels too tall compared to real red panda proportions, so I'm shortening the tail curve to peak around y 0.92-0.95 instead, recalculating the path points to compress the overall length to about 0.6 while keeping the same upward-curling silhouette. I'm also setting a tapering radius array across six keyframes so the tail starts slender at the base, thickens through the middle for a bushy look, and narrows again toward the tip.

Now I'm confirming the tail joint chain structure—five named segments parented to the hips with a "tail" role—lines up correctly with the six-point catmull path and sweep radius array, then moving on to color the body sweep with the coat paint.

I'm defining the head and jaw joints with their parent/aim orientations, then setting up the neck chain to sweep from the spine's tip, matching start points so the pieces connect seamlessly, before working out which spine joints the front and hind leg chains should parent to based on where the shoulders and hips sit along the body.

Now I'm placing the front leg root and target points with sensible lengths and bend directions so the elbow angles back naturally, then doing the same for the hind legs with a forward-knee bend typical of quadrupeds, figuring out the right format for the bends argument. I'm also setting sweep radii for each leg segment and planning a fur-edge color gradient so the upper hind thigh shows rust tones blending into the darker coat color.

Now I'm working out the body coat shading with orange on the back fading to dark on the belly and flanks using a fur-edge paint function, then moving into the head paint logic defining tear marks and brow patches based on distance from facial landmark points.

I'm layering cheek and muzzle cream patches, eye surround darkening, and deciding where cream, rust, and orange zones split across the face, plus adding small cream chin and crown tufts for the top of the head.

Now I'm working out the ear geometry, figuring out how the thickness direction mirrors between left and right ears and positioning the inner cream patch slightly forward so it's visible, then starting to paint the ear outline shapes.

I'm checking where the ear base attaches to the skull surface near the top, then placing the muzzle and nose spheres relative to the skull front, making sure the eye decals land correctly on the muzzle's width given its angle and elevation.

Given the slight overlap between the eye decal and muzzle edge, I'm nudging the eye position upward and widening it slightly to avoid clipping. I'm also sizing the skull to give the chibi head its oversized, rounded proportions relative to the body.

Now I'm placing cheek fur spikes and whisker rods with small symmetric offsets on each side of the face, then setting up the stone base joint parented to the hips with skinning left unaffected since the stone meshes stay rigid. I'm also double-checking that the stone's lathe profile and the ground lumps all sit flush at y=0 so nothing clips below the floor.

I'm scattering six rocky lumps using icosahedron geometry around the stone's edge with randomized angles and sizes, then refining the lathe profile points so the top radius matches where the feet rest, adjusting the foot ellipsoid height so its bottom aligns correctly with the stone surface.

Now I'm working out the front paw positions and sizes, placing them at the limb's target joint so the leg tip nests into the paw sphere, and adding a helper to resolve the chain's tip joint safely. I'm also setting up claw placement, offsetting each claw's base and tip slightly along the x-axis from the paw.

Adding toe spheres at the paw front to blend into the silhouette, then giving the hind legs bigger paws and a haunch bulge sphere near the hip joint for thigh definition.

Now I'm adding shoulder fluff and scattering moss cards across the stone surface and lumps, filtering for upward-facing points with minimum spacing, and splitting the hits into two color tints lit by surface normals. I'm also embedding flattened green moss sticks for solid bumps, and placing a handful of glowing octahedron motes at scattered positions around the body and tail for extra sparkle.

I'm defining the full color palette—orange, rust, cream, teal, gold, and various moss greens—then building a `tuftHits` helper and scattering body fur tufts using a seeded random filter, plus a cream neck bib using a fur-edge paint technique that blends colors based on surface normal direction with a toothy, periodic pattern along the body axis.

I'm reconsidering the axis orientation for the neck bib, since the tube points forward and up rather than straight up, so a normal threshold on z alone won't cleanly isolate the front/underside cream patch—thinking about whether a tilted axis vector or a position-based (y-coordinate) approach would better match where the bib should sit.

Then I'm planning the body loft radii sequence and sweep settings for the main coat, followed by the neck sweep's tapering radii, and adding a small collar loop detail at the base of the neck.

For the charm, I'm computing a hit point on the neck surface using azimuth/elevation around the tube, guarding for a null result, then embedding a small gold disc there with a teal gem offset slightly outward using the frame's moved position.

For the tassel, I'm offsetting from the charm hit downward to get a tip point and drawing a thin four-sided rod between the two, binding it to an explicit neck joint rather than letting it auto-attach. Before writing the final code, I'm double-checking which imports I actually need to use so nothing triggers an unused-import error — deciding to use INK for the nose color, and skipping unused helpers like frame or aim.

Now I'm sketching the leg construction: for each side, building front leg chains via inverse kinematics from shoulder to paw, attaching them to the spine, then sweeping a tapered tube along the chain for the coat shape. I'm doing the same for hind legs with hip-to-knee-to-foot points parented to the hips, and planning a separate paw function to build the paw geometry at the end of each limb.

Scattering card decoration across the tail surface, computing each card's position along the tail's curved spine path, orienting them to flow down and back along the tail with a lean and bend, and capping the tail tip with a dark rounded sweep. I'm also adding a sphere-based face/skull part scaled and positioned onto the head bone.

Now I'm defining the eye decals, placing iris and blush colors onto the skin using hit points around the head frame, mirrored for left/right sides, alongside a rust-brown eye patch marking. I'm then adding cream-colored ear tuft spikes positioned around the ear base and interior, specifying their direction, length, and radius for a few spikes per ear.

All these spikes get explicitly tied to the head bone, and I still need to work out the head joint's group and role assignment.
